query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A physics-informed machine-learning approach that explicitly accounts for 1 wt.% oxygen doping and real defect states will predict the thermal (or electrical) conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than conventional analytical models that assume a perfect, defect-free crystal lattice, across both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloy specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen, representative of real-world impurity levels.
generation.intervention: Adopt a hybrid defect-sensitive ML approach informed by ab initio simulations and existing temperature-dependent transport measurements on oxygen-doped samples.
generation.conditions: Compare predicted conductivity to measured values of both nominally ideal and 1 wt.% oxygen-doped bulk HfNbTaTiZr from near-0 K to 1200 K under controlled testing (e.g., in inert atmosphere, with incremental temperature increases).
generation.structural_mediator: Incorporation of oxygen defect sites that modify electron–phonon scattering and phonon transport, anchoring the ML training in partial experimental data and ab initio calculations.
generation.mechanism: Compositional and defect features captured by the ML model refine phonon-electron scattering and microstructural transport pathways, thus reducing systematic errors introduced by ideal-lattice assumptions in analytic predictions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduced prediction errors across the 0–200 K cryogenic region and 300–1200 K high-temperature range by about 15–25% relative to standard analytical methods that neglect defects.
generation.baseline: Existing analytical models of HfNbTaTiZr assuming a defect-free crystal, known to overestimate conductivity in oxygen-bearing samples by ~20% or more at cryogenic and elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: Approach is validated for HfNbTaTiZr with up to ~2 wt.% oxygen from about 0 K to 1200 K; applicability beyond these doping or temperature ranges remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: Limited calibration data above 1–2 wt.% oxygen or outside the 0–1200 K range leads to uncertainty in extrapolations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a new HfNbTaTiZr sample with a verified oxygen content near 1 wt.% but processed under different thermal/mechanical conditions than the training data. Measure conductivity from 5 K to 150 K and from 350 K to 1000 K, maintaining consistent experimental conditions. Compare results to model predictions trained on the existing dataset.
measurements: Thermal or electrical conductivity at intervals over 5–150 K and 350–1000 K
Microstructural characterization to confirm defect distributions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured conductivity deviates from the predicted values by more than 25% over more than half of the tested temperature range, the hypothesis that accounting for 1 wt.% oxygen doping within a physics-informed ML approach yields superior accuracy is falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted a lot of attention in recent years, due to the unique combinations of structural, physical and chemical properties of these alloys [1] – [3] . HEAs usually form simple structures such as body-centered cubic (BCC) (e.g. TaNbHfZrTi [4] , NbTaVWZr [5] etc.) or face-centered cubic (FCC) (e.g., CoCrCuFeNi [6] , CoCrFeMnNi [7] etc.) solid solutions. The large number of the alloying elements in near-equiatomic proportions result in high configurational entropy in these solid solutions. However, these alloys can decompose to multiple phases upon changing the composition or annealing at different temperatures or a combination of both [8] – [10] . Such a phase decomposition is often the result of the complex interplay of configurational entropy of mixing with the enthalpies of mixing of the constituent elements. Additionally, such multiphase microstructures are more likely to exhibit the desired properties for real engineering applications. Hence, tuning the composition and fractions of phases is critical for achieving the desired properties [10] , [11] .

The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

The computational software could significantly affect the efficiency of HTC since massive calculations are carried out. In the example of the Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system, it takes only a few hours on a desktop computer to finish the HTCs (~ 3 × 10 3 ) within the composition range of 5–50 at.% for each element and finally screen out eight potential alloys. chosen.lever: 1 wt.% O doping and any further compositional inhomogeneity
chosen.technique: Hybrid physics–ML approach combining defect-sensitive ab initio data with measured transport properties
chosen.conditions: Full temperature range (0–200 K and 300–1200 K), including known doping and real sample defects
chosen.why: This approach directly addresses the core question by tackling both the limited accuracy of analytic predictions and their reliance on idealized, defect-free structures. Incorporating measured data from oxygen-containing samples and known physical models into a machine learning framework can improve reliability and applicability across wide temperature regimes. This standard strategy in materials science—using ML to integrate experimental and computational insights—offers a clear path to verify and potentially falsify the new hypothesis via comparing predicted and measured conductivity for a held-out, differently doped or differently processed HfNbTaTiZr sample.
